title: the Panchadashi (selections)
hook: two glows through two doorways: a lamp and a jewel
tomorrow: a whole show, and nobody watches the lamp. why not?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Panchadashi's tenth traveler: the one counting was there all along. Today, two doorways, and an argument.

Some people won't start until they're sure: the right plan, the right major, the right words. Others start first and figure it out on the way. Inside Advaita, the same split shows up about meditation, and the Panchadashi answers with two doorways. In one room a lamp is burning. In the other, a jewel shines by its own light. Two people stand outside. Each sees a soft glow, and each thinks: a jewel. Both run in. Both were wrong about what they saw. Only one walks out rich.
screen: `START SURE, OR START NOW?` → `A LAMP. A JEWEL.` → `ONLY ONE WALKS OUT RICH.`

segments.voice: It's the one at the jewel's door. Same mistake, different glow. The book calls it an error that agrees with the truth, and it settles a real disagreement. One view, held firmly in Advaita: freedom comes only from knowing the self directly. Picturing Brahman, dwelling on a form or a quality like bliss or light, isn't that knowing. At its best, this view protects people from mistaking a pleasant state for the goal, and from spending a life polishing what was only ever a door. The other view, the one this chapter, the lamp of meditation, takes: meditation is chasing the glow of the real jewel. You may not see clearly what you're running toward, but you're running toward the right room. Steady, long meditation, the book says, can ripen into knowledge itself. Notice the Panchadashi doesn't throw out the first view. It agrees the glow isn't the gem. It simply won't scorn the person running toward it. So both voices stay at the table. One says: don't confuse the glow with the jewel. The other answers: but the glow is coming from the jewel.
screen: `AN ERROR THAT AGREES WITH THE TRUTH.` · `ONE VIEW: ONLY KNOWING FREES.` · `THE OTHER: THE GLOW LEADS IN.` · `BOTH STAY AT THE TABLE.` · then, large: `THE GLOW LEADS TO THE JEWEL.`

segments.voice: Choose one short word to say softly aloud on each out-breath: a name of God if you pray, the sound om, or a plain word like peace. Keep it slow and unhurried. When the mind wanders, come back to the same word, the way someone keeps walking toward the same glow.
The Panchadashi: today, the book that calls meditation a mistake worth making, because it follows the glow of the real jewel.
Hold on to it: the Panchadashi, where the glow of the real jewel leads to the jewel.

fork.setup: you side with the Panchadashi: meditation can ripen into knowledge. a friend holds the strict view. say that view's best case.
options: it guards against mistaking a calm state for the goal itself.
it says meditation is useless and nobody should do it.

fork.reveal: the strict view's strength is a warning: the glow isn't the gem. the Panchadashi agrees, and still honors the one running toward it.

chat.meaning: The Panchadashi keeps both views: the glow isn't the jewel, yet chasing the real jewel's glow can lead to it.

Panchadashi.meaning: a book of Advaita verses, credited to Vidyaranya

Advaita.meaning: not two: the view that self and Brahman are one

Brahman.meaning: the one reality the Upanishads point to

om.meaning: a sacred sound chanted in Hindu prayer and meditation

sources.ref: Panchadashi 9 (Dhyanadipa): the light of a gem and the light of a lamp, both mistaken for a gem; the one who goes to the gem's light gets the gem (samvadi bhrama, an error that agrees with the truth); meditation on Brahman can lead to knowledge

notes: Debate shape: both views inside Advaita speak in the teach (only direct knowing frees; meditation can ripen into knowing); the fork asks for the strict view's best case.
